frames.narration: Five tasks: A has no dependencies, B and C need A, D needs B and C, E needs D. A valid build order lists every task after the tasks it needs. A, B, C, D, E is one; A, C, B, D, E is another.
Kahn starts by counting unfinished dependencies for every task: A 0, B 1, C 1, D 2, E 1. Tasks with a count of 0 are ready, so only A goes into the queue.
Take A out of the queue and append it to the order. Then subtract one from each task that was waiting for A: B and C drop to 0 and join the queue. D still waits for two tasks.

B and C come out, and D's count falls from 2 to 1 to 0, so D is queued, then E. The order is A, B, C, D, E. Each task entered the queue once and each dependency was looked at once, so the work is tasks plus dependencies, not tasks squared.

The same pass gives levels: A is level 1, B and C level 2, D level 3, E level 4. B and C can run at the same time, so two workers finish in 4 steps instead of 5. The 4 levels are a floor: a third worker would change nothing.

Now someone makes B also depend on C. B and C wait for each other. After A, both counts stay at 1, the queue is empty and only 1 of 5 tasks is ordered. The cycle has 2 tasks but 4 are stuck, because D and E wait on them.

states.graph: B needs C, C needs B

frames.narration: Do not guess an order. A depth-first search over the stuck tasks follows the dependencies, meets B again while it is still on the current path, and so finds the cycle B, C, B. Report that path and fail the build, so a person fixes the real dependency.

A frequent shortcut is to rescan the whole task list for 'anything ready' after every pick. It works on 5 tasks and costs the square of the task count: 757,544 operations at 1,000 tasks against 5,046 for the queue. Keep a queue of ready tasks.
